title: Privileged Subset Data Escrow & Revocation Rider (Draft)
content:
Purpose and scope:
This Rider is intended to be appended to a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) or Master Services Agreement between Vendor and Customer to govern the temporary escrow, limited use, and rapid revocation of a narrowly defined privileged subset of Customer data (the "Privileged Subset") that Vendor may require for debugging, legal discovery, or security investigations. The rider focuses on minimization, custody, access controls, revocation mechanics, audit evidence, and operational timelines.

Key definitions (working list):
- Privileged Subset: the minimal set of Customer records, logs, or artifacts necessary to reproduce, investigate, or remediate a specific issue, scoped by ticket/incident id and time range.
- Custodian: an independent third-party escrow provider or internal Vendor role designated to hold the Privileged Subset under sealed controls.
- Escrow Token: ephemeral cryptographic token used to release data to authorized investigators.
- Revocation Event: any Customer request or automatic trigger requiring immediate access termination and verifiable destruction of the Privileged Subset.

Principles / high-level commitments (short):
- Data minimization: Vendor will only collect or escrow the smallest possible Privileged Subset and document scope in the intake record.
- Least privilege & just-in-time access: Access is time-limited, role-limited, and requires multi-factor approval.
- Verifiable revocation & tamper evidence: Customer can trigger revocation; Vendor must provide cryptographic and procedural evidence of revocation/destruction within committed timelines.
- Independent custody option: For high-risk customers, the Privileged Subset will be held by a Custodian under documented SLA.

Operational workflow (recommended template):
1) Intake and scope approval (T+0): Engineer opens incident ticket referencing Customer incident id. Intake form includes specific record identifiers, time ranges, and justification. Customer liaison must sign-off (can be delegated) for any non-emergency requests.
2) Minimal extraction (T+0 to T+2h): Vendor extracts only the fields/rows required, redacts PII beyond scope, and serializes into an encrypted archive (AES-256) tagged with the ticket id and custody metadata.
3) Escrow handoff (T+2h to T+6h): Archive is transferred to Custodian or Vendor sealed store. Metadata includes hash (SHA-256), extraction script version, and a purpose statement.
4) Access authorization (just-in-time): Access requires two privileged approvers (one engineering, one security/compliance). Access window defaults to 8 hours unless extended with additional approvals; extensions are auditable.
5) Investigation & ephemeral artifacts (during window): Any derivative artifacts (debug traces, redactions, summaries) must be labeled and recorded. Full copies may NOT be exported without Customer written consent.
6) Revocation and destruction (on request or at window end): On a Revocation Event, Vendor or Custodian must revoke tokens, zeroize keys where possible, and run a documented destruction procedure. Proof of destruction includes hash reconciliation, timestamped audit log, and operator signatures.

Evidence and audit items to deliver within SLA windows:
- Within 24 hours of revocation: signed destruction statement, destruction procedure runbook IDs, and SHA-256 pre/post hashes showing removal from active stores.
- Within 5 business days: escalation packet to Customer security contact with chain-of-custody logs, access approvals, extraction script snapshot (readonly), and Custodian confirmation (if applicable).
- On request: limited redacted sample of the original Privileged Subset to corroborate that data removed matches scoped identifiers (only if safe and approved).

SLA commitments (suggested):
- Emergency revocation response: initial acknowledgement within 1 hour, destruction evidence within 24 hours.
- Standard revocation: acknowledgement within 4 hours, destruction evidence within 72 hours.
- Audit packet delivery: within 5 business days.

Security controls (minimum):
- Encrypted-at-rest (AES-256) and in-transit (TLS 1.3).
- Hardware-backed key storage (KMS/HSM) with key lifecycle records. Keys enabling escrow access are rotated monthly; revocation must include key revocation steps.
- MFA for access approvers; separation of duties enforced via RBAC.
- Immutable append-only audit logs for custody events with exportable proofs.

Independent Custodian option (when Customer requests):
- Custodian is a mutually approved third party that stores encrypted archives and only releases data when (a) Customer and Vendor both approve, or (b) a court order is presented consistent with the primary agreement.
- Custodian SLA must include physical security, personnel background checks, and annual SOC2-type evidence.
- Custodian must provide signed notarized destruction certificates per request.

Revocation triggers (non-exhaustive list):
- Customer explicit request (written)
- End of authorized investigation window
- Completion of legal hold or litigation needs reconciled with Customer counsel
- Detection of unauthorized access or elevated risk to customer PII

Retention and reconstitution (end of matter):
- Unless otherwise agreed in writing, Privileged Subset copies held for investigations must be destroyed within 30 days of ticket closure.
- If a subset must be retained for legal hold, Vendor will log hold reason, retention period, and access restrictions. Customer may require Custodian retention under Customer-controlled keys for the hold duration.

Liability & indemnities (draft language):
- Vendor warrants that it will follow the operational workflow and technical controls above.
- For breaches caused by Vendor negligence in custody or revocation, Vendor will indemnify Customer for reasonable direct damages up to the limits in the parent agreement. (To be negotiated per enterprise).

Customer rights & remedies:
- Right to request a one-time on-site or remote verification (screen share) of destruction procedure within agreed hours.
- Right to require Custodian engagement for any Privileged Subset containing regulated personal data.
- Right to audit the custody logs (subject to mutual NDA) annually or on a triggered incident.

Template obligations for inclusion in parent contract (exhibit checklist):
- Exact definition of "Privileged Subset" and permitted fields
- Permitted uses and prohibited exports
- Custodian selection process and minimum controls
- Escrow Token lifecycle and revocation procedure (detailed steps)
- SLA timelines for acknowledgement and evidence delivery
- Evidence format (hashes, signed logs, destruction certificates)
- Escrow costs and billing treatment

Open items / TODOs (for legal & product teams):
- Finalize cryptographic proof-of-destruction format with engineering.
- Decide default access window duration (8h vs 24h).
- Align Custodian list with procurement and include template SOW.
- Add a small-claims remediation path for ephemeral-only leaks.

Notes for negotiators (practical tips):
- Customers often push for unlimited custody retention; we should counter with narrow timeboxes plus legal-hold carveouts.
- Independent Custodian reduces legal friction for enterprise security teams but adds cost; offer as paid add-on.
- Prefer operational evidence (hashes + logs) over blanket certifications; makes audits efficient.

Appendix: Suggested audit evidence schema (human-friendly):
- Ticket ID; Extraction script git sha; Customer signoff id; Archive SHA-256; Custodian receipt timestamp; Access approver ids; Access window timestamps; Destruction timestamp; Post-destruction archive SHA (empty or null) and operator signature.

(End of draft rider — working doc. Please add comments inline for legal language preferences and any jurisdictional constraints.)
